---
title: "N: Nervous system"
description: "ATC group N for modellers: the endpoint sets the structure, placebo and dropout need their own submodels, and PET occupancy bridges dose to effect."
date: "2026-02-08"
---

The level 2 codes in @tbl-atc-n-lvl-2 run from anaesthetics to other nervous system drugs, and the **endpoint**, not the drug, sets the model structure: processed EEG in N01 [@bjornssonTwoCompartmentEffectSite2010], daily seizure counts in N03 [@troconizModellingOverdispersionMarkovian2009] and bounded PANSS scores in N05 [@krekelsItemResponseTheory2017] each demand a different likelihood.

On 29 March 1948 John Cade gave lithium citrate to W.B., in manic excitement for five years; W.B. left hospital months later and returned to his old job [@cadeLithiumSaltsTreatment1949; @lopezmunozHistoryPharmacologicalTreatment2018].

| Level 2 code | Description |
| ---: | :--- |
| N01 | Anesthetics |
| N02 | Analgesics |
| N03 | Antiepileptics |
| N04 | Anti-Parkinson drugs |
| N05 | Psycholeptics |
| N06 | Psychoanaleptics |
| N07 | Other nervous system drugs |

: ATC N level 2 codes {#tbl-atc-n-lvl-2 tbl-colwidths="[20, 80]"}

## Modelling notes

**Endpoint.**
Analysing composite PANSS totals as continuous data discards information and violates the scale's numerical nature; item response theory models the items instead [@krekelsItemResponseTheory2017].
Depression trials have been modelled on the HAMD-17 total [@gomeniBayesianModellingROC2007].

**Placebo first.**
Placebo arms in schizophrenia and depression improve over weeks, so a placebo time course is fitted before estimating any drug effect [@pillareddyStructuralModelsDescribing2011].

**Dropout is informative.**
Dropout probability rises with a high observed PANSS score, so the dropout hazard is modelled jointly with the score as a [time-to-event](/docs/modeling/tte/) process [@pillareddyModellingSimulationPositive2012].
Ignoring it biases parameter estimates, though simulation put that bias relatively low; the model matters most for realistic trial simulation [@bjornsson2015dropout].

**Counts, not concentrations.**
Daily seizure counts in N03 are overdispersed and depend on the previous day, so negative binomial models with a Markov element beat Poisson [@troconizModellingOverdispersionMarkovian2009].
Add-on [exposure-response](/docs/modeling/pkpd/) is fitted on seizure rate, not a continuous score [@millerExposureResponseAnalysis2003].

**Anaesthesia is the hysteresis case.**
Processed EEG lags plasma concentration in N01, so the link is an effect site with an equilibration rate constant k~e0~ [@schniderInfluenceAgePropofol1999].
One effect compartment failed to describe the bispectral index across different propofol infusion rates; a two-compartment effect site succeeded [@bjornssonTwoCompartmentEffectSite2010].

**Easy to overlook.**
PET occupancy bridges dose and effect in N05: patients with acute extrapyramidal syndromes had higher D2 occupancy than those without [@fardePositronEmissionTomographic1992], and model-based analysis quantifies it against efficacy and those symptoms [@degreefDopamineD2Occupancy2011].

**Mechanistic extrapolation.**
Human CNS distribution data are scarce, so physiologically based models combined with microdialysis predict unbound extracellular concentrations at the target site [@yamamotoMicrodialysisKeyPhysiologically2017].
A separately developed paediatric brain PBPK model predicted CSF concentrations and was checked against CSF observed in children, meningitis included [@verscheijdenDevelopmentPhysiologicallyBased2019].
